html:
Stick charts are frames of palm ribs and shells made by navigators of the Marshall Islands to show how ocean swells bend and meet around islands. They were used until the mid-20th century.

Shells mark islands, and curved sticks show the swells that a navigator feels through the hull of a canoe. The charts were studied on land and not carried at sea. Each was made by and for a navigator, and the knowledge was kept secret in families.

Europeans first learned of them in the late 19th century. They show the skill behind Pacific navigation, the same skill revived by Hōkūleʻa. Canoe sailing schools in Majuro teach the old swell lore today. See also Marshall Islands.
